claims.text: When decisions are positive, interactional justice perceptions are significantly higher if the decision is made by a human rather than an AI.
When decisions are negative, there is no significant difference in interactional justice perceptions between human and AI decision makers.
For both positive and negative decisions, decision-maker role appropriateness perceptions are higher when decisions are made by a human rather than an AI.
For both positive and negative decisions, trust scores are higher when decisions are made by a human rather than an AI.
For both positive and negative decisions, dehumanization scores are lower when decisions are made by a human rather than an AI.
Irrespective of decision maker, receiving a positive valence outcome leads to higher interactional justice perceptions compared to a negative valence outcome.
Irrespective of decision maker, receiving a positive valence outcome leads to higher decision-maker role appropriateness perceptions compared to a negative valence outcome.
Irrespective of decision maker, receiving a positive valence outcome leads to higher trust scores compared to a negative valence outcome.
Irrespective of decision maker, receiving a positive valence outcome leads to lower dehumanization scores compared to a negative valence outcome.
Interactional justice perceptions are higher when an AI makes a positive decision compared to when a human makes a negative decision.

evidence.description: MANOVA post-hoc contrasts showed that for positive decisions, interactional justice was 3.88 for human decision makers versus 3.29 for AI decision makers (p < 0.001).
MANOVA post-hoc contrasts showed interactional justice mean was 3.06 for human decision makers versus 2.92 for AI decision makers when decisions were negative (no significant difference).
Role appropriateness scores were significantly higher for humans than AI for both positive decisions (5.49 vs 4.41) and negative decisions (4.55 vs 3.54) with p < 0.001.
Trust scores were significantly higher for human decision makers than AI decision makers for both positive outcomes (3.78 vs 3.31) and negative outcomes (2.98 vs 2.72) with p < 0.001.
Dehumanization scores were significantly lower for human decision makers than AI decision makers for both positive outcomes (2.53 vs 3.42) and negative outcomes (3.05 vs 3.62) with p < 0.001.
Interactional justice scores were significantly higher for positive outcomes than negative outcomes across both AI (3.29 vs 2.92) and human decision makers (3.88 vs 3.06) with p < 0.001.
Role appropriateness scores were significantly higher for positive decisions than negative decisions across both AI (4.41 vs 3.54) and human decision makers (5.49 vs 4.55) with p < 0.001.
Trust scores were significantly higher for positive decisions than negative decisions across both AI (3.31 vs 2.72) and human decision makers (3.78 vs 2.98) with p < 0.001.
Dehumanization scores were significantly lower for positive decisions than negative decisions across both AI (3.42 vs 3.62) and human decision makers (2.53 vs 3.05) with p < 0.001.
MANOVA post-hoc contrast showed interactional justice mean score was 3.29 for positive AI decisions compared to 3.06 for negative human decisions (p < 0.001).

methodologies.name: 2x2 Experimental Vignette Survey with MANOVA, Machine Learning, and Thematic Analysis
methodologies.description: A 2x2 experimental survey study manipulating decision maker (AI vs human) and outcome valence (positive vs negative) across six HRM functions, analyzed using MANOVA, C5.0 classification decision trees, and qualitative thematic coding.
datasets: CloudResearch North American working adult sample (N=446)
conditions: AI decision maker / negative valence outcome
AI decision maker / positive valence outcome
Human decision maker / negative valence outcome
Human decision maker / positive valence outcome

limitations.text: The experimental vignette methodology decontextualizes the decision-making phenomenon and does not capture workplace context factors such as leadership quality, institutional policies, or broader job satisfaction.
The experimental design focused on manipulating decision maker and decision valence, which sidelined salient aspects of AI such as explainability and computational transparency.
Existing research into justice perceptions of AI decision making in the workplace largely focuses on procedural and distributive forms of justice, neglecting interactional justice.

future_work.text: Examine whether embodied AI forms, such as chatbots and avatars, alter interactional justice perceptions compared to unembodied software-based AI.
Investigate how manipulating the amount and form of explanations provided by whitebox AI systems enhances or diminishes informational and interactional justice perceptions.
Replicate the research across different regulated high-risk contexts, such as healthcare decision making.
